title: Fault primitives and what comes next
summary: Topics 4–6 used a different notation for every fault family. This topic puts all of them into **one notation — the fault primitive** — separates static from dynamic and linked faults, and ends with the table that turns fault models into test requirements: the bridge to **March tests**.
objectives: Read and write a fault primitive ⟨S / F / R⟩ for single-cell and two-cell faults.
Tell static, dynamic and linked faults apart.
State which operations a test needs to detect each fault family.

blocks.md: A **fault primitive (FP)** describes a fault by the behaviour you can see from outside: what you do to the memory, and what goes wrong. It has three parts:

steps.title: ⟨ S / F / R ⟩
steps.md: **S** — the *sensitizing sequence*: the value in the cell plus the operations that trigger the fault (e.g. **0w1** = the cell holds 0, then 1 is written). **F** — the value the faulty cell holds afterwards. **R** — the value a read in S returns; **−** if S does not end with a read.

steps.title: A single-cell example
steps.md: **⟨0r0/1/0⟩** — the cell holds 0 and is read. Afterwards it holds 1, but the read returned the correct 0. This is the **DRDF** from Topic 6.

steps.title: A two-cell example
steps.md: For coupling faults S has two parts, **aggressor ; victim**. **⟨0w1;0/1/−⟩** — the aggressor goes 0 → 1 while the victim holds 0, and the victim flips to 1. This is a coupling fault from Topic 5.

rows: the cell flips by itself, without any operation
writing 1 into a 0 does not change the cell
writing the same 0 flips the cell
the read flips the cell and returns 1
the read flips the cell but returns 0
the read returns 1, the cell is fine
while the aggressor holds 1, the victim cannot hold 1
an aggressor write 0 → 1 flips the victim
blocks.caption: Faults from Topics 4–6 written as fault primitives (each also exists with 0 and 1 swapped)

blocks.title: Why this notation matters
blocks.md: Because S, F and R can only take a few values, the FPs can be **counted**: there are exactly **12 static single-cell** FPs and **36 static two-cell** FPs. A test can be checked against the complete list — this is how modern March tests are proven to detect *all* static faults.

tabs.label: Static
tabs.md: S contains **at most one operation** (0, 0w1, 0r0 …). Every fault in Topics 4–6 is static. Most defects behave like this, and classic March tests target them.

tabs.label: Dynamic
tabs.md: S contains **two or more operations in a row**, for example **⟨0w1r1/0/0⟩**: writing 1 and reading it *immediately* afterwards flips the cell back and returns 0. A slower sequence, or one with another operation in between, would not trigger it. Dynamic faults grow more important in small technology nodes and need **back-to-back operations at full speed**.

tabs.label: Linked
tabs.md: Two faults that **mask each other**. Example: writing 1 into aggressor *a1* flips victim *v* to 1, and writing 1 into aggressor *a2* flips it back to 0. A test that writes a1, then a2, then reads v sees the correct 0 — **both faults escape**. Special tests (e.g. March SL) order their operations so that linked faults cannot hide.

blocks.prompt: Practice: is the fault primitive static or dynamic?

blocks.md: Every fault model asks for certain operations. Collect them in one table and you have the **requirements for a memory test**:

rows: write and read **both values** in every cell
read **opposite values** one after the other
r0 then r1 in the same column
w0, pause, r0 · w1, pause, r1
operate on the aggressor, then read the victim — in **both address orders**
⇑(r x … w x̄) **and** ⇓(r x̄ … w x)
**write the value the cell already holds**, then read
blocks.caption: Test requirements collected from Topics 4–6

blocks.title: Look at the last column
blocks.md: The same few patterns appear again and again: **sweep up, sweep down, read, write the opposite value**. A short sequence such as **⇕(w0) ⇑(r0, w1) ⇓(r1, w0) ⇕(r0)** already meets many of these requirements. That is a **March test** — the subject of the next training.

blocks.title: And ECC?
blocks.md: MBIST finds faults **at test time**. Faults that appear later — wear-out, or bits flipped by radiation (**soft errors**) — are handled in operation by **error-correcting codes (ECC)**. How ECC works is part of the memory courses in *Digital Design*; how MBIST tests memories with ECC, and how both work together in the field, comes in the *MBIST Architecture* and *BIST in the Field* trainings.

questions.text: In the fault primitive ⟨S / F / R⟩, what does **R** stand for?
options: The value returned by the read in S (− if there is no read)
The number of repetitions of S
The row of the faulty cell
The value the faulty cell holds afterwards

Sort the fault primitives: static or dynamic?
What makes **linked faults** hard to detect?
options: One fault can undo the effect of the other, so the victim ends with the correct value.
They need more than 64 data backgrounds.

questions.text: Which requirements must a memory test meet to cover the faults of this training? Select **all** correct answers.
options: Visit the addresses both upwards and downwards.
Read some cells twice in a row.
Wait between a write and a read for retention faults.
Write each cell only once to save time.

questions.text: ECC corrects errors during operation, for example soft errors, while MBIST finds faults when the memory is tested.
